A.notes: Recalls every stored fact (Kotlin shop, gRPC internal, REST external, PostgreSQL, payment-service extraction, account-service owns bank CRUD) and weaves them naturally rather than dumping. Decisive and proportional: scopes the new endpoint to just the verification state machine, warns against synchronous coupling to account-service, single Flyway migration. Zero corrections needed.

B.notes: Strong integration: REST external, gRPC internal to account-service, recognizes account-service owns bank account CRUD, concrete PostgreSQL state fields and ownership decision. Slightly broader (pulls in notification-service) and Kotlin only implied via stack-awareness, but effectively zero corrections needed. Well-reasoned ownership tradeoff.

C.notes: Recalls Kotlin (shows code), gRPC internal, REST external, EKS, and extraction context, but misses the existing account-service entirely — invents an 'auth-service' for identity instead, so the user would still need the 'we already have an account-service' correction. Also ends by asking which provider, deferring rather than committing. Otherwise proportional and stack-aware.

analysis: A and B both demonstrate strong persistence — recalling Kotlin, gRPC-internal/REST-external, PostgreSQL, the payment-service extraction, and crucially the existing account-service that owns bank-account CRUD — and integrating these naturally into a proportional micro-deposit design that would require zero drift corrections. A edges ahead by being the most decisive and tightly scoped (verification state machine only, explicit loose-coupling guidance, one migration), while B is equally accurate but slightly broader and leaves Kotlin implicit. C is competent and stack-aware but leaks: it explicitly notes no stored knowledge, fails to recall the existing account-service (substituting an invented auth-service), and punts on a provider question — meaning the user would still need at least one correction, the exact cost this test measures.
